hypothesis: The dominant premise that an interpreter/dispatch layer is the gas problem for chaining multicall VMs is misdirected: for the workloads these VMs actually run (DeFi compositions dominated by external CALLs to AMMs, lending pools, and SLOAD/SSTORE-heavy targets), the marginal gas of a thin assembly dispatch + return-data wiring (mcopy/MLOAD/MSTORE) is a single-digit-percent overhead that is dwarfed and routinely net-negative versus the alternative of multiple separately-signed transactions or naive multicall, because (a) per-opcode arithmetic/memory costs are tiny next to CALL + cold/warm storage costs and (b) the very block-level superoptimization the literature validates can be applied once to the interpreter's hot path. The right lever for gas is therefore optimizing the called targets and storage access pattern, not eliminating the dispatch layer.
rationale: The gas-optimization literature in the corpus establishes that provable, machine-verified savings live at the basic-block / memory-operation level and that storage opcodes dominate cost budgets — 'A Max-SMT Superoptimizer for EVM handling Memory and Storage' explicitly extends superoptimization to memory operations as the missed opportunity, and 'GASOL: Gas Analysis and Optimization for Ethereum Smart Contracts' offers cost models that isolate storage opcodes as the heavy contributors. 'MadMax: surviving out-of-gas conditions in Ethereum smart contracts' frames gas blow-ups as arising from unbounded loops and storage, not from per-instruction dispatch. 'Inferring Needless Write Memory Accesses on Ethereum Bytecode' shows memory-write elimination is a concrete, automatable win — directly applicable to an interpreter's mcopy-based return wiring. Meanwhile the only on-point interpreter paper, 'MultiCall: A Transaction-batching Interpreter for Ethereum,' exists precisely to amortize per-transaction overheads. The contrarian claim is that these threads jointly imply the dispatch tax is second-order: optimize the hot path once (Max-SMT/GASOL-style) and spend the engineering budget on storage access, not on stripping composability.
supports_if: A controlled microbenchmark of a Weiroll-class chaining VM vs. equivalent native/EOA-sequenced calls on realistic DeFi targets shows the interpreter+wiring overhead is <~10% of total gas and is net-negative once base-transaction (21k) and re-approval/re-transfer costs are counted; and applying Max-SMT/GASOL-style block optimization to the dispatch hot path closes most of the remaining gap. The two-line abstracts' emphasis on storage/memory as the dominant cost would be vindicated by a measured cost breakdown putting CALL+storage >>> dispatch arithmetic.
refutes_if: Measured breakdowns show the dispatch/decoding/return-wiring layer is itself a large (>25-30%) and irreducible share of gas on representative workloads, OR that block-level superoptimization (per the Max-SMT/GASOL results) cannot be applied to the data-dependent dispatch path and so the overhead persists — i.e., the interpreter tax is first-order and the 'too expensive' view is correct.
motivating_papers: MultiCall: A Transaction-batching Interpreter for Ethereum
A Max-SMT Superoptimizer for EVM handling Memory and Storage
GASOL: Gas Analysis and Optimization for Ethereum Smart Contracts
MadMax: surviving out-of-gas conditions in Ethereum smart contracts
Inferring Needless Write Memory Accesses on Ethereum Bytecode

hypothesis: Full formal verification is the WRONG default answer for a chaining multicall VM. The decisive safety property is not the VM interpreter's whole-program correctness (which is small, loop-free, and amenable to one-time block-level verified optimization) but the composed economic behavior of the attacker-chosen sequence of external calls the VM enables — a property the corpus's heavyweight verifiers (VerX, eThor, KEVM-based provers) are structurally ill-suited to discharge because it is cross-contract, value/MEV-dependent, and data-flow-dynamic. The evidence supports a split design: (1) verify the tiny dispatch core once with block-optimization-grade proofs, and (2) defend the composed scripts with economic/non-interference properties and fuzzing, NOT with contract-level functional verification.
rationale: Two corpus threads collide here. First, verification's reach and adoption are limited: surveys and challenge papers repeatedly flag soundness/scalability/adoption gaps — 'Ethereum Smart Contract Analysis Tools: A Systematic Review,' 'A Survey on Formal Verification for Solidity Smart Contracts,' and 'On the Formal Verification of Smart Contracts and Blockchain: Challenges and Future Directions' — while flagship verifiers like 'VerX: Safety Verification of Smart Contracts' explicitly scope to 'a practical fragment' of contracts and 'eThor: Practical and Provably Sound Static Analysis of Ethereum Smart Contracts' trades completeness for soundness. These tools target single-contract functional/safety properties, not adversarial cross-contract value flows. Second, the genuinely matching threat model for composed calls is economic: 'DeFi Composability as MEV Non-interference' and 'Formal Analysis of Composable DeFi Protocols' formalize harm as interference between a compound service and its dependencies — exactly what a chaining VM amplifies — and 'On the Just-In-Time Discovery of Profit-Generating Transactions in DeFi Protocols' shows the attack surface is sequence/value search, not interpreter bugs. The corpus also shows the VM core itself is verifiable cheaply and locally: 'Formally Verified EVM Block-Optimizations' and 'Secure Optimizations on Ethereum Bytecode Jump-Free Sequences' verify exactly the loop-free, jump-free fragment a dispatch hot path is. Contrarian synthesis: pour verification effort into the small core and into economic non-interference of scripts; do not chase full functional verification of the whole VM/composition.
supports_if: A case study finds that historically impactful failures of chaining/composed transactions stem from economic composition (price manipulation, sandwich/JIT, dependency interference) rather than interpreter-logic bugs; that the dispatch core is small/loop-free enough to be fully verified with 'Formally Verified EVM Block-Optimizations'-class techniques at low cost; and that MEV-non-interference-style or fuzz-based properties catch composition hazards that VerX/eThor-style single-contract verification provably cannot express.
refutes_if: Evidence shows the interpreter/dispatch core is itself a recurring source of exploitable bugs that contract-level functional verifiers (VerX/eThor/KEVM-based) DO catch in practice, OR that economic non-interference properties are not checkable/useful for these VMs — i.e., full formal verification of the VM and its scripts is both necessary and sufficient, making the split-design contrarian claim wrong.

hypothesis: The presumed three-way trade-off (gas vs. expressiveness vs. verifiability) is not a hard frontier but an artifact of choosing the EVM's stack machine plus hand-rolled, schema-less bit-packed offset encoding as the substrate. A register/IR-style chaining design with an explicitly specified operational semantics collapses the trade-off: it can be simultaneously more gas-stable, more expressive, AND more verifiable than a stack-based interpreter, because the data-flow wiring becomes first-class (named registers / SSA-like result slots) rather than opaque memory offsets. The contrarian claim is that the host project's biggest verifiability/gas risk is the hand-rolled offset encoding, not the interpreter concept, and that the evidence favors deriving the VM from a formal semantics rather than retrofitting verification onto bit-packed assembly.
rationale: The corpus contains a direct architectural comparison — 'A Performance Survey on Stack-based and Register-based Virtual Machines' — and 'VM Matters: A Comparison of WASM VMs and EVMs in the Performance of Blockchain Smart Contracts,' which together undercut the assumption that the EVM stack model is the performance-optimal substrate. 'IELE: An Intermediate-Level Blockchain Language Designed and Implemented Using Formal Semantics' is the existence proof for the contrarian claim: its abstract states the VM was generated FROM a formal specification and that its register-based design choices were driven by problems observed formalizing the EVM — i.e., verifiability and a cleaner data-flow model were obtained together, not traded off. 'An Operational Semantics for Yul' and 'Formal and Executable Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine in Dafny' show that explicit, executable semantics for EVM-family languages are now routine, and 'Formally Verified EVM Block-Optimizations' / 'ByteSpector: A Verifying Disassembler for EVM Bytecode' show verified reasoning over EVM code fragments is tractable. Against this, the host project (per AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) relies on a hand-rolled 256-bit offset layout with NO shared schema and a stated pitfall that the layouts must be kept in sync by hand — precisely the kind of opaque, semantics-free wiring that the IELE/operational-semantics line argues against. Contrarian thesis: spend design budget on a semantics-derived, register/slot-based wiring (verifiable + expressive + gas-stable) rather than treating the trade-off as inherent to interpreters.
supports_if: An IELE/register-style or SSA-slot chaining design (with an explicit operational semantics in the style of 'An Operational Semantics for Yul' / the Dafny EVM semantics) is shown to encode the same DeFi chains with equal-or-better gas AND a machine-checkable wiring invariant, while the bit-packed offset scheme is shown to be the actual source of cross-layer bugs/verification difficulty (Solidity-decoder vs. JS-encoder drift). 'A Performance Survey on Stack-based and Register-based Virtual Machines' would predict no inherent gas penalty for the register-style data flow.
refutes_if: A register/IR-style or semantics-derived chaining VM is shown to cost materially more gas on-chain than the stack/offset approach for equivalent chains (because EVM execution is itself stack-based, taxing any non-stack abstraction), OR the bit-packed offset encoding is shown to be straightforwardly verifiable and not a bug source — in which case the trade-off is real and the EVM-native stack+offset design is justified.
